blocks.text: Carnival in Rio: long green feathers and a gem-studded headdress

blocks.text:
This route combines the Carnival Champions Parade in Rio with a journey through Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Bolivia and Peru. Over 18 days, you will travel from the Atlantic and Iguazu Falls to Buenos Aires, Santiago and the Atacama Desert, then climb onto the Bolivian Altiplano, cross Uyuni and finish at Lake Titicaca, Cusco, Machu Picchu and Lima.

This route is for travellers who want to see the main cities, natural sights and highland regions of several countries in one trip.

## Carnival and a journey across the continent

Your first days are in Rio. You will see the city from the ocean and from its two main viewpoints: Sugar Loaf and Corcovado. Between these excursions comes the central event of the trip, the Champions Parade at the Sambadrome.

Carnival becomes part of the city here, extending beyond an evening show. By day, Rio is a city of beaches, bays, old neighbourhoods and granite hills. At night, the Sambadrome fills with drums, floats, costumes and samba schools that have spent the whole year preparing for this appearance.

After Rio, the journey continues to Iguazu. On the Brazilian side, the falls gradually come into view as a broad panorama. The Argentine side brings you closer to the water: walkways run above the currents, below the cascades and towards the Devil’s Throat.

Buenos Aires brings back the pace of the city. Plaza de Mayo, La Boca, San Telmo, Recoleta and Puerto Madero follow one another on a single guided tour, with a tango show and dinner in the evening.

The next major stage starts in Chile. Santiago introduces you to its historic centre and modern districts, then a flight to Calama takes you to the Atacama. The urban landscape gives way to dry air, volcanoes, desert plains and the night sky.

From San Pedro de Atacama, the route climbs onto the Bolivian Altiplano. You spend several days travelling by jeep among coloured lagoons, geysers, hot springs and volcanoes. This part of the journey culminates at the Uyuni Salt Flat.

La Paz brings you back to city life, briefly. The road to Peru passes through Tiwanaku and Lake Titicaca, followed by the final part of the journey: Puno, Cusco, Machu Picchu and Lima.

## Why the route feels like five different journeys

The Brazilian section centres on water and tropical greenery. Rio lies between the ocean and the mountains, while Iguazu is surrounded by humid forest. The scenery changes completely even within one country.

Argentina is represented by Buenos Aires. Here the focus shifts to architecture, old neighbourhoods, city history and tango. After several days by the ocean and waterfalls, the change of setting is clear.

Chile begins in Santiago, but the main transition comes after the flight to Calama. In the Atacama, the air becomes drier, vegetation all but disappears, and mountains and volcanoes remain on the horizon.

Bolivia brings the most expedition-like part of the route. Laguna Verde, the Dalí Desert, Polques, Sol de Mañana and Laguna Colorada lie among open highland landscapes. You spend the night in a simple desert hotel, then continue by jeep towards Uyuni.

Peru closes the route with Inca history and the Pacific Ocean. The floating Uros Islands, the road from Puno to Cusco, Machu Picchu, Qorikancha and Sacsayhuamán gradually lead you to Lima, where the ocean returns after the highlands.

## What you will see along the way

Rio reveals itself gradually. On the first day, take time to get a feel for the city without a guided schedule: head to the ocean, walk along the wave-patterned mosaic promenade and see how a vast city fits between granite hills and the water. The perspective changes the following day. The cable car climbs Sugar Loaf, bringing bays, beaches, islands and the Niterói Bridge into a single panorama.

By the evening of the second day, the city looks quite different. The Sambadrome becomes a long, illuminated stage for the samba schools. First comes the sound of percussion, followed by the marching groups, costumes and floats. The stands respond to familiar songs and colours, and the parade continues until morning. The following day is therefore devoted to Corcovado, without an additional evening programme.

The ascent to Corcovado passes through Tijuca Forest. The humid forest almost touches the train carriages, with brief glimpses of the city between the trunks. At the top, Christ the Redeemer no longer looks like a small figure above Rio. In front of the statue, you can see the bay, Sugar Loaf, Maracanã and the city’s complex geography between water and hills.

Foz do Iguaçu changes the sound as well as the scenery. You still have to travel through the forest to reach the falls, but the roar of the water can be heard before you arrive. On the Brazilian side, the path keeps its distance, gradually revealing the entire line of cascades. Individual white torrents form a broad system, and the final walkway approaches the Devil’s Throat.

The Argentine side offers a different experience. The upper route passes above the water before it falls; the lower route shows individual cascades from the side and below. Walkways cross the broad river towards the Devil’s Throat. Access to some viewing platforms may change with the water level.

Buenos Aires offers a short break between the natural sections. Plaza de Mayo and the Casa Rosada reveal the official centre, San Telmo and La Boca the old neighbourhoods, and Puerto Madero the modern waterfront. In the evening, a tango show with a live orchestra shifts the focus from architecture to music and movement.

After the flight to Santiago, the journey gradually turns towards the Andes. The city remains a large modern centre, but the mountains are a constant presence in the panorama. Santa Lucía Hill shows this contrast particularly clearly: the city centre below, modern districts beyond, and the Andes in the distance.

The Atacama brings an abrupt change from the cities. After Calama, the road crosses a landscape with almost no vegetation. San Pedro de Atacama is low-rise, surrounded by volcanoes, salt-covered areas and dry plains. At night, the absence of bright city lighting makes the sky the main sight. The optional astronomical tour makes use of these conditions.

The following day marks the beginning of the expedition section. After the Bolivian border, you change to jeeps and drive to Laguna Verde. Next come the Dalí Desert, Polques, Sol de Mañana and Laguna Colorada. Familiar urban landmarks are almost absent here: open plateaus, rock, unusually coloured water, steam and volcanoes fill the landscape.

Uyuni changes your sense of distance even further. In dry weather, the salt surface is covered with geometric patterns. After rain, a thin layer of water reflects the sky, making the horizon almost disappear. This change explains why photographs of the same salt flat can look so different.

After several days of desert landscapes, La Paz brings you back to a dense urban setting. The Witches’ Market remains part of living local culture. The Moon Valley, by contrast, almost removes the city from view despite being nearby: its pointed earth formations feel like a separate world.

Tiwanaku provides a historical transition to Peru. The Gate of the Sun, the monoliths and Kalasasaya belong to a civilisation that existed before the Incas. The border, Puno and Lake Titicaca then lead into the next part of Andean history.

On the Uros Islands, the ground is made by hand. Totora reeds provide the material for both the floating islands and the boats. The surface gives underfoot, and residents regularly add new layers as the lower ones become waterlogged and break down.

The road from Puno to Cusco is an excursion in its own right. Stops at Andahuaylillas, Raqchi, La Raya and Pucará make the journey more than a transfer. You approach Cusco gradually, through a series of cultural and natural sights.

Machu Picchu comes after a long sequence of countries and altitudes. The road leads towards greener, more humid slopes. First, individual walls and terraces appear among the clouds, followed by the whole city fitted into the ridge. The contrast with Uyuni and the Atacama, visited only a few days earlier, is clear.

The final day in Lima brings you back to the Pacific Ocean. The Parque del Amor stands on the high coast, before the route turns into the historic centre and ends at the Larco Museum. After 18 days through five countries, this is a calm finish before your transfer to the airport.

## Altitude, climate and pace

The route crosses very different altitudes. After coastal Rio and Buenos Aires, the journey gradually enters the Andes. San Pedro de Atacama comes before the ascent to the Altiplano, where some points lie above 4,000 m.

The Bolivian section calls for a particularly measured approach to exertion. You travel by jeep, the desert accommodation is simple, and the climate is considerably drier and colder than at the beginning of the trip. After La Paz, the high-altitude section continues at Lake Titicaca and on the road to Cusco.

The included programme varies in intensity. Flights and transfers provide occasional breaks, and some guided tours take 3–4 hours. This sequence allows you to see a great deal while varying the pace.

## What you can add

At Iguazu, you can add the Bird Park for USD 50 per person and the Macuco Safari for USD 130.

In Santiago, you can add visits to Maipo Valley wineries for USD 230 per person, with a minimum of 2 participants.

An astronomical tour is available in the Atacama. It costs USD 350 per person, with a minimum of 2 participants.
